1	package netdiag
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"net/netip"
6		"time"
7	
8		"charm.land/bubbles/v2/textinput"
9		tea "charm.land/bubbletea/v2"
10		"github.com/charmbracelet/x/ansi"
11	
12		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/nettrace"
13		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/components"
14		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/datatable"
15		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/shortcut"
16		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/theme"
17	)
18	
19	const (
20		// reasonPathUnsupported is shown when the platform cannot trace a path. The
21		// header greys enter out and the handler refuses with the same text.
22		reasonPathUnsupported = "The path trace is not supported on this platform"
23	
24		// defaultPathResolveTimeout bounds the name resolution of a target.
25		defaultPathResolveTimeout = 5 * time.Second
26	
27		// pathInputCharLimit holds a 253-character host name, a colon and a port.
28		pathInputCharLimit = 262
29	)
30	
31	// pathState is where the Path tab is in its life cycle.
32	type pathState int
33	
34	const (
35		// pathEditing: the target field has the keyboard.
36		pathEditing pathState = iota
37		// pathRunning: a trace is in flight; the field is blurred.
38		pathRunning
39		// pathDone: a trace ended (or was canceled); the hops stay on screen.
40		pathDone
41	)
42	
43	// PathModel is the Path tab: a target field above a table of hops that fills
44	// in while the trace runs.
45	type PathModel struct {
46		width  int
47		height int
48	
49		engine         pathEngine
50		resolveTimeout time.Duration
51	
52		input textinput.Model
53		table datatable.Model[pathStep]
54	
55		state  pathState
56		target pathTarget
57		addr   netip.Addr
58		// route is the way out of this machine; nil until the resolved message.
59		route *pathRoute
60		// hops is what the engine reported so far; the table shows
61		// visiblePathHops(hops). At done it is replaced by Result.Hops.
62		hops   []nettrace.Hop
63		result *nettrace.Result
64		// errText is the persistent footer error of a run that never traced. It is
65		// cleared by a change of the field or by the next launch, not by a timer.
66		errText string
67	
68		// gen identifies the run whose messages are accepted; cancel and msgs
69		// belong to that run.
70		gen    int
71		cancel context.CancelFunc
72		msgs   <-chan tea.Msg
73	
74		footer components.FooterMessage
75	
76		// source is where the trace starts: this machine, or a running container
77		// (DEVDESK-330). picker is the open selector, nil when closed; sourcesGen
78		// identifies the listing whose answer it accepts; container is what the
79		// column says about the source of the current run.
80		source     pathSource
81		picker     *pathSourcePicker
82		sourcesGen int
83		container  *pathContainer
84	}
85	
86	// pathSourceKey opens the "Trace from" selector (declared exception, surface
87	// netdiag/path).
88	const pathSourceKey = "ctrl+o"
89	
90	// pickerOpen reports whether the selector holds the keyboard.
91	func (pm *PathModel) pickerOpen() bool { return pm.picker != nil }
92	
93	func newPathModel(e pathEngine) *PathModel {
94		in := textinput.New()
95		theme.StyleTextInput(&in)
96		in.Placeholder = "hostname or IPv4 address[:port]"
97		in.CharLimit = pathInputCharLimit
98		in.Focus()
99	
100		return &PathModel{
101			engine:         e,
102			resolveTimeout: defaultPathResolveTimeout,
103			input:          in,
104			table: datatable.New(datatable.Config[pathStep]{
105				Columns:    pathColumns(),
106				SortColumn: -1, // the path order is the content
107			}),
108		}
109	}
110	
111	// InEditMode reports whether the target field has the keyboard.
112	// The open selector holds the keyboard too, from any state.
113	func (pm *PathModel) InEditMode() bool { return pm.state == pathEditing || pm.pickerOpen() }
114	
115	func (pm *PathModel) running() bool { return pm.state == pathRunning }
116	
117	func (pm *PathModel) resize(width, height int) {
118		pm.width = width
119		pm.height = max(height, 3)
120		pm.input.SetWidth(max(width-ansi.StringWidth(pathBarLabel)-4, 10))
121		pm.table.Resize(width, pm.height)
122	}
123	
124	// launchable is the one answer to "can a trace start here", read by the header
125	// and by the handler (Rule 130).
126	func (pm *PathModel) launchable() shortcut.Availability {
127		if pm.engine.supported() != nil {
128			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonPathUnsupported)
129		}
130		return shortcut.Availability{}
131	}
132	
133	func (pm *PathModel) update(msg tea.Msg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
134		switch msg := msg.(type) {
135		case pathResolvedMsg:
136			return pm.handleResolved(msg)
137		case pathHopMsg:
138			return pm.handleHop(msg)
139		case pathDoneMsg:
140			return pm.handleDone(msg)
141		case pathSourcesMsg:
142			return pm.handleSources(msg)
143		case tea.KeyPressMsg:
144			return pm.handleKey(msg)
145		case tea.PasteMsg:
146			return pm.handlePaste(msg)
147		}
148		// Anything else is a footer expiry or the cursor blink of the field: the
149		// field needs the blink itself, or its cursor freezes.
150		pm.footer.Handle(msg)
151		var cmd tea.Cmd
152		pm.input, cmd = pm.input.Update(msg)
153		return pm, cmd
154	}
155	
156	func (pm *PathModel) handleResolved(msg pathResolvedMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
157		if msg.gen != pm.gen {
158			return pm, nil
159		}
160		pm.addr = msg.addr
161		route := newPathRoute(msg.route, msg.routeErr)
162		pm.route = &route
163		if !msg.source.isHost() {
164			c := newPathContainer(msg.source, msg.ctr, msg.ctrErr).withBridgeRead(msg.bridge)
165			pm.container = &c
166		}
167		pm.refreshSteps()
168		return pm, waitForPathMsg(pm.msgs)
169	}
170	
171	func (pm *PathModel) handleHop(msg pathHopMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
172		if msg.gen != pm.gen {
173			return pm, nil
174		}
175		pm.hops = append(pm.hops, msg.hop)
176		pm.refreshSteps()
177		return pm, waitForPathMsg(pm.msgs)
178	}
179	
180	func (pm *PathModel) handleDone(msg pathDoneMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
181		if msg.gen != pm.gen {
182			return pm, nil
183		}
184		pm.releaseRun()
185		if msg.err != nil {
186			pm.hops = nil
187			pm.route = nil
188			pm.container = nil
189			pm.table.SetItems(nil)
190			pm.errText = pathErrorLabel(pm.target.Host, msg.err)
191			pm.state = pathEditing
192			return pm, pm.input.Focus()
193		}
194		res := msg.result
195		pm.result = &res
196		pm.hops = res.Hops
197		pm.refreshSteps()
198		pm.state = pathDone
199		return pm, nil
200	}
201	
202	// refreshSteps rebuilds the table rows from the route and the hops.
203	func (pm *PathModel) refreshSteps() { pm.table.SetItems(pathSteps(pm.container, pm.route, pm.hops)) }
204	
205	// clearRun forgets what the last run put on screen: the resolved address, the
206	// route, the container, the hops, the outcome and the error.
207	func (pm *PathModel) clearRun() {
208		pm.addr = netip.Addr{}
209		pm.hops = nil
210		pm.route = nil
211		pm.container = nil
212		pm.result = nil
213		pm.errText = ""
214		pm.table.SetItems(nil)
215	}
216	
217	// hopCount is the number of hop rows (the local rows are not counted).
218	func (pm *PathModel) hopCount() int {
219		n := 0
220		for _, s := range pm.table.Items() {
221			if s.Kind == stepHop {
222				n++
223			}
224		}
225		return n
226	}
227	
228	// releaseRun cancels the run's context (releasing it) and forgets its channel.
229	func (pm *PathModel) releaseRun() {
230		if pm.cancel != nil {
231			pm.cancel()
232			pm.cancel = nil
233		}
234		pm.msgs = nil
235	}
236	
237	func isPathNavKey(key string) bool {
238		switch key {
239		case "up", "down", "pgup", "pgdown", "home", "end":
240			return true
241		}
242		return false
243	}
244	
245	func (pm *PathModel) handleKey(msg tea.KeyPressMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
246		key := msg.String()
247		if pm.pickerOpen() {
248			return pm.handlePickerKey(key)
249		}
250		if key == pathSourceKey {
251			return pm.openPicker()
252		}
253		if isPathNavKey(key) {
254			return pm, pm.table.Update(msg)
255		}
256		switch pm.state {
257		case pathEditing:
258			return pm.handleEditKey(msg)
259		case pathRunning:
260			if key == "esc" {
261				return pm.cancelRun()
262			}
263		case pathDone:
264			switch key {
265			case "enter":
266				return pm.launch(pm.target)
267			case "esc":
268				pm.state = pathEditing
269				return pm, pm.input.Focus()
270			}
271		}
272		return pm, nil
273	}
274	
275	func (pm *PathModel) handleEditKey(msg tea.KeyPressMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
276		switch msg.String() {
277		case "enter":
278			return pm.launchFromInput()
279		case "esc", "tab", "shift+tab":
280			return pm, nil
281		}
282		return pm.updateInput(msg)
283	}
284	
285	func (pm *PathModel) handlePaste(msg tea.PasteMsg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {

287			return pm, nil // a paste reaches the focused field only (Rule 111)
288		}

292	// updateInput hands msg to the field; a changed value drops the stale error.
293	func (pm *PathModel) updateInput(msg tea.Msg) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
294		before := pm.input.Value()
295		var cmd tea.Cmd
296		pm.input, cmd = pm.input.Update(msg)

298			pm.errText = ""
299		}

303	func (pm *PathModel) launchFromInput() (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
304		tg, err := parsePathTarget(pm.input.Value())
305		if err != nil {
306			return pm, pm.footer.Error(capitalize(err.Error()))
307		}
308		return pm.launch(tg)
309	}

311	// launch starts a run: the model changes here, in Update; the Cmd only does I/O.
312	func (pm *PathModel) launch(tg pathTarget) (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
313		if a := pm.launchable(); !a.Enabled() {
314			return pm, pm.footer.Warn(a.Reason)
315		}
316		pm.releaseRun()
317		pm.gen++
318		pm.target = tg
319		pm.clearRun()
320		pm.footer.Clear()
321	
322		ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
323		ch := make(chan tea.Msg, pathChanCap)
324		pm.cancel, pm.msgs = cancel, ch
325		pm.input.Blur()
326		pm.state = pathRunning
327		return pm, startPathRun(ctx, pm.gen, tg, pm.source, pm.resolveTimeout, pm.engine, ch)
328	}

330	// cancelRun answers esc at once: the run's late messages are dropped by the
331	// generation bump, the hops already seen stay on screen.
332	func (pm *PathModel) cancelRun() (*PathModel, tea.Cmd) {
333		pm.releaseRun()
334		pm.gen++
335		pm.result = &nettrace.Result{Outcome: nettrace.OutcomeCancelled}
336		pm.state = pathDone
337		return pm, nil
338	}

340	// startPathRun builds the launch Cmd from values only, so that no closure
341	// reads the model (Rule 110).
342	func startPathRun(ctx context.Context, gen int, tg pathTarget, src pathSource, timeout time.Duration, e pathEngine, ch chan tea.Msg) tea.Cmd {
343		return tea.Batch(
344			func() tea.Msg {
345				producePath(ctx, gen, tg, src, timeout, e, ch)
346				return nil
347			},
348			waitForPathMsg(ch),
349		)

1240	`producePath` asks `pathEngine.route` for the traced address. The system
1241	engine uses `netcheck.SystemEnv(netcheck.DefaultSettings()).Route`, which sends
1242	nothing and needs no privilege. The answer (`RouteHop`: interface, source,
1243	gateway) rides on `pathResolvedMsg` (`route`, `routeErr`), so there is no extra
1244	message and the capacity stays 32. `newPathRoute` turns it into a `pathRoute`
1245	(addresses unmapped to IPv4). The lookup asks the kernel the same question as
1246	`ip route get <addr>` (go-netroute, `RTM_GETROUTE`, policy rules applied), and
1247	the probe socket is unmarked and not bound to a device, so a VPN that captures
1248	the default route shows as the interface row, and the probes take that route.
1249

1	package netdiag

3	import (
4		"fmt"

9		"path/filepath"
10		"slices"

12		"strings"
13		"testing"
14	)
15	
16	// DEVDESK-330 criterion 7, view level: the Path tab reaches the container
17	// engine only through a fixed list of read functions, and no source file of the
18	// package names a verb that starts, creates or enters a container. The runtime
19	// half is TestPathEngineReadsStartNothing.
20	//
21	// What the guard sees: selectors on the docker and engine packages (aliases
22	// included, dot imports refused), string literals and constant concatenations
23	// and fmt.Sprint* calls over literals whose words include a forbidden verb
24	// (case-insensitive, per word: "container START abc" is caught, UI prose such
25	// as "Run again" is not), imports of
26	// os/exec, execabs, syscall, calls to os.StartProcess, and any internal
27	// package that is not on allowedInternalImports.
28	//
29	// What it does not see, by construction: a verb assembled from variables or
30	// read at run time (a config value, an environment variable, strings.Join over
31	// a slice, a rune loop), and a read function of the docker package that itself
32	// starts something (the allowed list is the contract; those functions are
33	// covered by internal/docker's own tests and by the runtime half).
34	
35	const (
36		dockerImportPath   = "github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/docker"
37		engineImportPath   = "github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/engine"
38		internalImportBase = "github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/"
39	)
40	
41	// allowedDockerUses is every docker.<X> the Path tab may name: the read
42	// functions and the types they return.
43	var allowedDockerUses = []string{
44		"Container", "ContainerNetworking", "EndpointNetwork",
45		"ListContainersContext", "EngineOperatingSystem", "InspectContainerNetworking",
46		"IsContainerID", "NetworkBridge", "InspectNetworkBridge",
47	}
48	
49	// allowedEngineUses is every engine.<X> the Path tab may name.
50	var allowedEngineUses = []string{"Current"}
51	
52	// allowedInternalImports is every internal package the netdiag sources import.
53	// A new one fails the guard so that it is looked at once: a package that can
54	// reach the engine or a process must not slip in through a helper.
55	var allowedInternalImports = []string{
56		"command", "config", "docker", "engine", "forward", "jobs", "netcheck",
57		"netiface", "nettrace", "ports", "shared",
58		"ui/components", "ui/datatable", "ui/help", "ui/indicator", "ui/keymap",
59		"ui/overlay", "ui/shortcut", "ui/theme",
60	}
61	
62	// forbiddenImports start processes: the Path tab has no business with them.

# Accessing network applications with WSL | Microsoft Learn

There are a few considerations to be aware of when working with networking apps and WSL. By default WSL uses a NAT based architecture, and we recommend trying the new Mirrored networking mode to get the latest features and improvements.

## Identify IP address

There are two scenarios to consider when identifying the IP address used for a Linux distribution running via WSL:

**Scenario One:** From the perspective of the Windows host, you want to query a Linux distribution's IP address running via WSL2, so that a program on Windows host can connect to a server program running inside the distribution (instance).

The Windows host can use command:

```powershell
wsl.exe --distribution <DistroName> hostname -I
```

If querying the default distribution, this part of the command designating the distribution can be omitted: `-d <DistroName>`. Be sure to use a lower-case `-i` flag.

Under the hood, host command wsl.exe launches the target instance and executes Linux command `hostname --all-ip-addresses`. This command then prints the IP address of the WSL instance to `STDOUT`. The `STDOUT` text content is then relayed back to wsl.exe. Finally, wsl.exe displays that output to the command line.

A typical output might be:

```powershell
172.30.98.229
```

**Scenario Two:** A program running inside a Linux distribution via WSL2 (instance) wants to know the Windows host's IP address, so that a Linux program can connect to a Windows host server program.

The WSL2 Linux user can use command:

```bash
ip route show | grep -i default | awk '{ print $3}'
```

A typical output might be:

```powershell
172.30.96.1
```

So the `172.30.96.1` is the host IP address for Windows, in this example.

Note

These above IP address querying action is typically required when WSL2 is running with the default NAT network mode. When the WSL2 is running with the new mirrored mode, the Windows host and WSL2 VM can connect to each other using `localhost` (127.0.0.1) as the destination address, so the trick of using a query peer's IP address is not required.

## Default networking mode: NAT

By default, WSL uses a NAT (Network Address Translation) based architecture for networking. Keep the following considerations in mind when working with a NAT-based networking architecture:

### Accessing Linux networking apps from Windows (localhost)

If you are building a networking app (for example an app running on a NodeJS or SQL server) in your Linux distribution, you can access it from a Windows app (like your Edge or Chrome internet browser) using `localhost` (just like you normally would).

### Accessing Windows networking apps from Linux (host IP)

If you want to access a networking app running on Windows (for example an app running on a NodeJS or SQL server) from your Linux distribution (ie Ubuntu), then you need to use the IP address of your host machine. While this is not a common scenario, you can follow these steps to make it work.

1. Obtain the IP address of your host machine by running this command from your Linux distribution:

    ```bash
    ip route show | grep -i default | awk '{ print $3}'
    ```
2. Connect to any Windows server using the copied IP address.

The picture below shows an example of this by connecting to a Node.js server running in Windows via curl.

![Connect to NodeJS server in Windows via Curl](media/wsl2-network-l2w.png)

### Connecting via remote IP addresses

When using remote IP addresses to connect to your applications, they will be treated as connections from the Local Area Network (LAN). This means that you will need to make sure your application can accept LAN connections.

For example, you may need to bind your application to `0.0.0.0` instead of `127.0.0.1`. In the example of a Python app using Flask, this can be done with the command: `app.run(host='0.0.0.0')`. Keep security in mind when making these changes as this will allow connections from your LAN.

### Accessing a WSL 2 distribution from your local area network (LAN)

When using a WSL 1 distribution, if your computer was set up to be accessed by your LAN, then applications run in WSL could be accessed on your LAN as well.

This isn't the default case in WSL 2. WSL 2 has a virtualized ethernet adapter with its own unique IP address. Currently, to enable this workflow you will need to go through the same steps as you would for a regular virtual machine. (We are looking into ways to improve this experience.)

Here's an example of using the [Netsh interface portproxy](/en-us/windows-server/networking/technologies/netsh/netsh-interface-portproxy) Windows command to add a port proxy that listens on your host port and connects that port proxy to the IP address for the WSL 2 VM.

```powershell
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=<yourPortToForward> listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=<yourPortToConnectToInWSL> connectaddress=(wsl hostname -I)
```

In this example, you will need to update `<yourPortToForward>` to a port number, for example `listenport=4000`. `listenaddress=0.0.0.0` means that incoming requests will be accepted from ANY IP address. The Listen Address specifies the IPv4 address for which to listen and can be changed to values that include: IP address, computer NetBIOS name, or computer DNS name. If an address isn't specified, the default is the local computer. You need to update the `<yourPortToConnectToInWSL>` value to a port number where you want WSL to connect, for example `connectport=4000`. Lastly, the `connectaddress` value needs to be the IP address of your Linux distribution installed via WSL 2 (the WSL 2 VM address), which can be found by entering the command: `wsl.exe hostname -I`.

So this command may look something like:

```powershell
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=4000 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=4000 connectaddress=192.168.101.100
```

To obtain the IP address, use:

- `wsl hostname -I` for the IP address of your Linux distribution installed via WSL 2 (the WSL 2 VM address)
- `cat /etc/resolv.conf` for the IP address of the Windows machine as seen from WSL 2 (the WSL 2 VM)

Using `listenaddress=0.0.0.0` will listen on all [IPv4 ports](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9987409/want-to-know-what-is-ipv4-and-ipv6#:%7E:text=The%20basic%20difference%20is%20the,whereas%20IPv6%20has%20128%20bits.).

Note

Using a lowercase "i" with the hostname command will generate a different result than using an uppercase "I". `wsl hostname -i` is your local machine (127.0.1.1 is a placeholder diagnostic address), whereas `wsl hostname -I` will return your local machine's IP address as seen by other machines and should be used to identify the `connectaddress` of your Linux distribution running via WSL 2.

## IPv6 access

- `wsl hostname -I` for the IP address of your Linux distribution installed via WSL 2 (the WSL 2 VM address)
- `ip route show | grep -i default | awk '{ print $3}'` for the IP address of the Windows machine as seen from WSL 2 (the WSL 2 VM)

Using `listenaddress=0.0.0.0` will listen on all [IPv4 ports](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9987409/want-to-know-what-is-ipv4-and-ipv6#:%7E:text=The%20basic%20difference%20is%20the,whereas%20IPv6%20has%20128%20bits.).

## Mirrored mode networking

On machines running Windows 11 22H2 and higher you can [set `networkingMode=mirrored` under `\[wsl2\]` in the `.wslconfig` file](wsl-config#configuration-settings-for-wslconfig) to enable mirrored mode networking. Enabling this changes WSL to an entirely new networking architecture which has the goal of 'mirroring' the network interfaces that you have on Windows into Linux, to add new networking features and improve compatibility.

Here are the current benefits to enabling this mode:

- IPv6 support
- Connect to Windows servers from within Linux using the localhost address `127.0.0.1`. IPv6 localhost address `::1` is not supported
- Improved networking compatibility for VPNs
- Multicast support
- Connect to WSL directly from your local area network (LAN)

Note

Run the following command in PowerShell window with admin privileges to [Configure Hyper-V firewall](/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/network-security/windows-firewall/hyper-v-firewall) settings to allow inbound connections:

```powershell
Set-NetFirewallHyperVVMSetting -Name '{40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}' -DefaultInboundAction Allow
```

or

```powershell
New-NetFirewallHyperVRule -Name "MyWebServer" -DisplayName "My Web Server" -Direction Inbound -VMCreatorId '{40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}' -Protocol TCP -LocalPorts 80
```

This new mode addresses networking issues seen with using a NAT (Network Address Translation) based architecture. Find known issues or file feedback on any bugs identified in the [WSL product repo on GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL).

## DNS Tunneling

On machines running Windows 11 22H2 and higher the `dnsTunneling` feature is on by default (which can be found [under `\[wsl2\]` in the `.wslconfig` file](wsl-config#configuration-settings-for-wslconfig)) and it uses a virtualization feature to answer DNS requests from within WSL, instead of requesting them over a networking packet. This feature is aimed to improve compatibility with VPNs, and other complex networking set ups.

## Auto Proxy

On machines running Windows 11 22H2 and higher, setting [`autoProxy=true` under `\[wsl2\]` in the `.wslconfig` file](wsl-config#configuration-settings-for-wslconfig) enforces WSL to use Windows' HTTP proxy information. If you have a proxy already set up in Windows, enabling this feature will make that proxy be set automatically in WSL as well.

## WSL and firewall

On machines running Windows 11 22H2 and higher, with WSL 2.0.9 and higher, the Hyper-V firewall feature will be turned on by default. This will ensure that:

- See [Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security](/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/network-security/windows-firewall/windows-firewall-with-advanced-security) to learn more about Windows security features that will automatically apply to WSL.
- See [Configure Hyper-V firewall](/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/network-security/windows-firewall/hyper-v-firewall) to learn more about applying these rules and settings both locally and via online tools like Intune.

# DEVDESK-333 (S-07) : reconnaître WSL2 et étiqueter la source et le premier saut

Plan de conception seulement : aucun fichier modifié.

## Questions bloquantes

**Q1. Peut-on lancer `wslinfo` depuis l'onglet Path ?**
- **Pourquoi c'est bloquant.** Le spike n'a trouvé qu'un signal qui prouve le mode **NAT** : `wslinfo --networking-mode` (W2, `spike-wsl.md`), et c'est un programme externe. Or la garde `internal/ui/netdiag/path_engine_source_guard_test.go` interdit `os/exec` et n'accepte que les paquets internes de sa liste `allowedInternalImports`, pour qu'aucun paquet capable de lancer un processus n'entre par un helper.
- **Option A (recommandée).** Un nouveau paquet `internal/wslenv` lance `wslinfo`, avec :
  - un chemin absolu fixe (`/usr/bin/wslinfo`, puis `/usr/sbin/wslinfo`), sans recherche dans `PATH` ;
  - un seul argument constant, `--networking-mode` ;
  - un délai de 2 s ;
  - un lancement seulement quand WSL est déjà détecté : Linux natif ne lance jamais rien.
  
  On recoupe le résultat avec la présence de l'interface `loopback0`. Dans le spike, elle existe en mirrored et pas en NAT (`ip -br link`). C'est aussi le signal qu'utilise Moby (Docker) pour reconnaître le mode mirrored sans lancer `wslinfo`. Si les deux signaux ne concordent pas, le mode est indéterminé.
  
  Coût : `wslenv` est ajouté à `allowedInternalImports`, ce qui est une exception à la garde, faite à dessein.
- **Option B (aucun processus lancé).** Mirrored est reconnu par `loopback0`. Pour NAT, deux variantes :
  - B1 : NAT est toujours « indéterminé ». Le critère 2 n'est alors jamais rempli.
  - B2 : NAT est déduit de l'absence de `loopback0`. Les autres modes (par exemple `virtioproxy`, `none`) n'ont pas été mesurés, et le critère 5 interdit de deviner.
- **Recommandation : A.** Le plan ci-dessous suppose A. Avec B, l'étape 2 perd le lancement de `wslinfo` et le critère 2 tombe.

## Signaux de détection retenus

| Question | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Est-ce WSL ? | `WSL_DISTRO_NAME` non vide **ou** `/proc/sys/kernel/osrelease` contient `microsoft` (sans tenir compte de la casse) | Signal déjà utilisé par `internal/browser`, `internal/clipboard` et `internal/ui/terminal`. Le fichier couvre le cas `env -i`, où la variable disparaît (mesure `env -i PATH=` du spike). |
| WSL2 plutôt que WSL1 ? | `osrelease` contient `WSL2` (mesuré : `6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2`) | spike-wsl. WSL1 est hors périmètre (S-08) : s'il n'y a pas de preuve de WSL2, on n'affiche aucune mention WSL. |
| Quel mode ? | Sortie de `wslinfo` (`nat` ou `mirrored`), qui doit concorder avec `loopback0` (absente en NAT, présente en mirrored). Tout autre cas donne « indéterminé » : erreur, délai dépassé, binaire absent, autre valeur, désaccord. | W2 (une lecture en NAT, quatre en mirrored) ; [Moby `wsl2_linux.go`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/wsl2_linux.go) |
| Quelle est la passerelle du NAT ? | La route par défaut de la table principale, lue dans `/proc/net/route` (lecture de fichier, pas de processus) | [Microsoft Learn, NAT](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/networking) : en NAT, la passerelle par défaut est l'IP de l'hôte Windows. Mesuré par W3 : `172.27.128.1` est à la fois la passerelle et l'adresse de `vEthernet (WSL)`. |

**Règle d'étiquette « Windows host (virtual switch) ».** L'étiquette n'est posée que si toutes ces conditions sont vraies :
- WSL2 est prouvé ;
- le mode est NAT ;
- la passerelle du NAT est valide ;
- la route du trace a pour passerelle la passerelle du NAT ;
- la route du trace sort par l'interface de cette route par défaut.

Elle est alors posée sur la ligne `gateway` et sur le saut de TTL 1 si son adresse est cette passerelle. Un VPN dans la distro qui passe par le routage par politique (wg-quick) ou par des routes `def1` (OpenVPN) ne remplit pas ces conditions : pas d'étiquette.

## Plan (étapes TDD)

**Étape 1. `internal/wslenv`, partie pure (S).** Pas de dépendance.
- **Fichiers.** `wslenv.go`, `classify.go`, `procroute.go` et leurs tests.
- **Interfaces.**
  ```go
  type Mode int // ModeUndetermined, ModeNAT, ModeMirrored
  type Facts struct { DistroName, OSRelease, NetworkingMode string; NetworkingModeErr error; Interfaces []string; ProcNetRoute []byte }
  type Info struct { WSL2 bool; Mode Mode; NATInterface string; NATGateway netip.Addr }
  func Classify(f Facts) Info
  func defaultGateway(procNetRoute []byte) (iface string, gw netip.Addr, ok bool)
  ```
- **Tests (table).**
  - Linux natif (`6.12.0-amd64`, pas de variable) : `WSL2=false`.
  - Faits NAT du spike : `ModeNAT`, gateway `172.27.128.1` sur `eth0`.
  - Faits mirrored du spike : `ModeMirrored`, `NATGateway` invalide.
  - `nat` avec `loopback0` présente : indéterminé. `mirrored` sans `loopback0` : indéterminé.
  - Erreur de `wslinfo`, ou valeur `virtioproxy` : indéterminé.
  - `env -i` (variable vide, `osrelease` WSL2) : `WSL2=true`.
  - `osrelease` WSL1 `4.4.0-19041-Microsoft` : `WSL2=false`.
  - `defaultGateway` : hexadécimal little-endian (`01801BAC` donne `172.27.128.1`), plusieurs routes par défaut (la métrique la plus basse gagne), aucune route, ligne malformée (`ok=false`).
- **Fin.** `go test ./internal/wslenv` passe sous Windows et sous Linux.

**Étape 2. `internal/wslenv`, lectures système (M).** Dépend de l'étape 1.
- **Fichiers.** `detect.go`, `wslinfo.go`, `detect_test.go`, `source_guard_test.go`, `live_linux_test.go` (`//go:build linux`).
- **Interfaces.**
  ```go
  type Probe struct { GOOS string; Getenv func(string) string; ReadFile func(string) ([]byte, error); InterfaceNames func() ([]string, error); NetworkingMode func(ctx context.Context) (string, error) }
  func SystemProbe() Probe
  func Gather(ctx context.Context, p Probe) Facts
  func Detect(ctx context.Context) Info
  ```
- **Tests (sonde factice qui compte les appels).**
  - `GOOS=windows` : aucun appel.
  - Linux natif : `NetworkingMode` et la lecture de `/proc/net/route` ne sont jamais appelés.
  - WSL : un seul appel à `wslinfo`.
  - Une erreur de `ReadFile` équivaut à une valeur vide.
  - Un contexte annulé donne un mode indéterminé.
  - La sortie de `wslinfo` est bornée à 64 octets et nettoyée des espaces.
- **Garde de source.** `os/exec` n'apparaît que dans `wslinfo.go`, avec les chemins et l'argument constants. Modèle : `internal/nettrace/source_guard_test.go`.
- **Test réel.** Ignoré si WSL est détecté ; sinon `Detect` rend `WSL2=false`.

**Étape 3. Lignes de la colonne (S).** Dépend de l'étape 1 ; **parallélisable avec l'étape 2.**
- **Fichiers.** Nouveau `internal/ui/netdiag/path_wsl.go` (pur), `path_steps.go` (deux champs et le texte des cellules), `path_wsl_test.go`.
- **Interfaces.**
  ```go
  func withWSL(steps []pathStep, info wslenv.Info) []pathStep // returns a new slice; input untouched
  func windowsHostGateway(info wslenv.Info, r pathRoute) (netip.Addr, bool)
  ```
  `pathStep` gagne `WSL wslenv.Info` (lu par la ligne source) et `WindowsHost bool` (ligne gateway et saut de TTL 1). La signature de `pathSteps` ne change pas : elle a 9 appels dans les tests, que rien ne touche.
- **Tests par critère.**
  - **C1.** WSL2 (tous modes) : la ligne source vaut `WSL2 (VM), not the Windows host · <mode>`, et plus `this machine`. Même chose avec une source conteneur.
  - **C2.** NAT, saut de TTL 1 = passerelle : la cellule du saut et celle de la gateway valent `172.27.128.1 — Windows host (virtual switch)`. Si le TTL 1 est muet, la gateway seule est étiquetée. Si l'interface ou la passerelle de la route diffère de la passerelle du NAT, aucune étiquette.
  - **C3.** Mirrored, même avec saut de TTL 1 = gateway : `· mirrored mode`, et aucune cellule ne contient `Windows host`.
  - **C4.** Info vide (Linux natif) : aucune cellule ne contient `WSL` ni `Windows`, et le résultat est identique à `pathSteps` seul.
  - **C5.** Indéterminé : `· WSL2 mode undetermined`, sans étiquette Windows.
  - Plus : `withWSL` ne modifie pas son entrée, et l'étiquette ne va jamais sur un saut de TTL supérieur à 1.

**Étape 4. Branchement du flux (S).** Dépend des étapes 1 à 3.
- **Fichiers.** `path_run.go`, `path_model.go`, `path_engine_source_guard_test.go`, `header.go` (aide), `path_run_test.go`, `path_flow_test.go`.
- **Changements.**
  - `pathEngine` gagne `platform func(ctx context.Context) wslenv.Info`. Dans `systemPathEngine`, il vaut `wslenv.Detect`. Si le champ est nil (les fakes actuels), on prend l'info vide.
  - `producePath` l'appelle avant l'envoi du message résolu, sous `resolveTimeout`. Le résultat voyage dans `pathResolvedMsg.platform` : pas de nouveau message, la capacité reste 32.
  - `PathModel` gagne `platform wslenv.Info`. `handleResolved` le fixe ; `clearRun` et la fin en erreur le remettent à zéro. `refreshSteps` applique `withWSL(pathSteps(...), pm.platform)`.
  - `"wslenv"` est ajouté à `allowedInternalImports`, avec un commentaire qui renvoie à Q1.
  - Une ligne d'aide Path, en anglais US.
- **Tests.**
  - Un faux `platform` NAT : l'info arrive sur le message résolu et les lignes C2 apparaissent.
  - `platform` est appelé une fois par lancement.
  - Une run périmée (`gen`) n'applique pas son info.
  - Un relancement efface l'info précédente.
  - `mise run test-race` passe.

**Étape 5. Documentation (S).** Dépend de l'étape 4.
- `docs/architecture/network.md` : nouvelle section WSL2 avec signaux, règle d'étiquette et limites ; corriger « The source is never a host name ».
- `docs-site/docs/explanation/network.md`.
- La liste des fonctions de l'onglet Path dans `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
- `brief.md` : les libellés S-07 deviennent décidés.
- Une décision dans `docs/backlog.md` (exception à la garde, signaux), à archiver par l'archivist.

## Hypothèses (choix prudents, à valider par le ux ou l'utilisateur sans bloquer)

- Le mode s'affiche en suffixe de la ligne source (`· NAT mode`, `· mirrored mode`, `· WSL2 mode undetermined`), pas dans une ligne à part.
- L'étiquette va aussi sur la ligne `gateway` : c'est la même preuve que pour le saut de TTL 1.
- Si WSL est détecté sans preuve de WSL2 (noyau personnalisé), on n'affiche aucune mention WSL. Le grisage de WSL1 reste à S-08.
- La ligne `trace`, `from this machine (host or WSL VM)` (S-06), ne change pas.
- La détection se refait à chaque lancement, sans cache : quelques ms, et seulement sous WSL.

## Risques

- **Irréversible, ou presque :** un processus lancé depuis l'onglet Path (Q1). Garde-fous : chemin absolu, argument constant, délai, lancement seulement sous WSL, garde de source.
- `loopback0` et `wslinfo` n'ont été mesurés que sur WSL 2.7.13.0. Si Microsoft les change, ou sur un WSL antérieur à 2.0.4 (pas de `wslinfo`), le mode devient indéterminé. Ça échoue du côté sûr.
- L'étiquette NAT repose sur la conception documentée de WSL et sur W3, mesuré sur une seule machine. Risque résiduel : un VPN dans la distro qui remplace la route par défaut de la table principale ferait étiqueter le tunnel à tort.
- Le TTL 1 est parfois muet (spike, relance L4). Le saut n'est alors pas étiqueté ; la ligne gateway porte l'étiquette.
- La ligne source passe à environ 50 caractères : à vérifier par les tests de mise en page (`path_column_layout_test.go`) et en terminal étroit.

Sources :
- [Microsoft Learn, Accessing network applications with WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/networking)
- [moby/moby `daemon/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/wsl2_linux.go`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/wsl2_linux.go)
- Dans le dépôt : `docs/product/network-map/spike-wsl.md` (W2, W3), `feasibility.md`, `brief.md` (libellés S-07)

Fichiers lus : `C:\Users\anthoni\projects\entire\anthnel\devdesk\internal\ui\netdiag\path_steps.go`, `path_run.go`, `path_model.go`, `path_view.go`, `path_engine_source_guard_test.go`, `C:\Users\anthoni\projects\entire\anthnel\devdesk\docs\architecture\network.md`.

- Si WSL est détecté sans preuve de WSL2 (noyau personnalisé), on n'affiche aucune mention WSL. Le grisage de WSL1 reste à S-08.
- La ligne `trace`, `from this machine (host or WSL VM)` (S-06), ne change pas.
- La détection se refait à chaque lancement, sans cache : quelques ms, et seulement sous WSL.

## Risques

- **Irréversible, ou presque :** un processus lancé depuis l'onglet Path (Q1). Garde-fous : chemin absolu, argument constant, délai, lancement seulement sous WSL, garde de source.
- `loopback0` et `wslinfo` n'ont été mesurés que sur WSL 2.7.13.0. Si Microsoft les change, ou sur un WSL antérieur à 2.0.4 (pas de `wslinfo`), le mode devient indéterminé. Ça échoue du côté sûr.
- L'étiquette NAT repose sur la conception documentée de WSL et sur W3, mesuré sur une seule machine. Risque résiduel : un VPN dans la distro qui remplace la route par défaut de la table principale ferait étiqueter le tunnel à tort.
- Le TTL 1 est parfois muet (spike, relance L4). Le saut n'est alors pas étiqueté ; la ligne gateway porte l'étiquette.
- La ligne source passe à environ 50 caractères : à vérifier par les tests de mise en page (`path_column_layout_test.go`) et en terminal étroit.
